chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar quoted Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ahmad ibn al-Nadhr al-Khazzaz, on the authority of Amr ibn Shamar, on the authority of Jabir al-Ja'fi, on the authority of Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) cursed ten [groups] in relation to wine: its planter, its caretaker, its presser, its drinker, its server, its carrier, the one to whom it is carried, its seller, its buyer, and the one who consumes its price.

key_terms.آكِلُ ثَمَنِهَا: The one who consumes/eats its price (the seller who receives payment)
key_terms.الْخَمْر: Wine (specifically grape wine, often used as a metonym for all intoxicants)
key_terms.سَاقِيهَا: The server (who pours and serves the wine)
key_terms.عَاصِرُهَا: The presser (who squeezes the grapes to extract juice)

ai.seo_question: Who are the ten people cursed in relation to wine according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Al-Khisal*, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) expands the prohibition of wine beyond mere consumption to encompass the entire economic and logistical chain, including growers, carriers, and sellers. This comprehensive curse underscores the Shia jurisprudential view that wine is a source of communal impurity, justifying the inclusion of all stakeholders in the divine curse. It reflects the holistic approach to *khamr* in Shia fiqh, where the act of drinking is intrinsically linked to the acts of producing and trading it.
